issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, the trigger 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile clinically unless there is additional trauma content involving female perpetrators or a separate interpersonal trauma; nothing else in the profile supports that specific gendered trigger.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: 'When people say things like my ex' implies a salient intimate-relationship trauma context that is not reflected anywhere else in the threat, memory, appraisal, or strategy items, making it a poor fit with the stated index trauma of terrorism.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after terrorism, but phrasing the event as happening 'because of the way I acted' suggests a strong personal-causation formulation. With the rest of the profile centered on external danger, startle, flashbacks, and monitoring others, this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported and sits awkwardly with the terrorism trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger item about 'my ex' is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of terrorism and the rest of the profile. It implies an intimate-relationship trauma context rather than reminders of a terrorist event, whereas the other trigger items (old photos, alcohol smell) and threat items are trauma-related.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the terrorism trauma context as presented here. In the absence of any terrorism-specific circumstance suggesting personal responsibility, 'The event happened because of the way I acted' implies causal responsibility for the attack, which is clinically implausible for this patient profile and not supported by the other selected items.

vignette: At fifty-seven, Linh spent the evening at a downtown restaurant celebrating a colleague's retirement when the coordinated explosions tore through the dining room. The initial blast knocked her against a marble pillar, followed by a second concussion that rattled the ceiling fixtures. She crawled through shattered glass and overturned chairs, guiding panicked patrons toward the stairwell until her knees gave out on the sidewalk. The air grew heavy with the sharp, sweet tang of spilled whiskey and wine. Survivors huddled against a brick wall, phones raised to capture the smoke-choked facade and the dazed faces of people they recognized from the guest list. When police officers approached, they asked her to recount the sequence of events. Linh spoke through shaking hands until her voice fractured, the words feeling like broken glass in her throat, and she stopped answering questions entirely after the third night. Since that evening, her body has not settled. At her studio, she is suddenly pulled back into the dining room-not as a recollection, but as a visceral reliving. The floor tilts, the scent of burning insulation fills her nose, and her muscles lock as if preparing to dodge falling debris. When her husband reaches for her shoulder in the hallway, she flinches so violently she knocks a ceramic bowl off the counter. She has learned to anticipate contact, stepping back before anyone can brush past her. On the subway to client site visits, she scans the car's interior, cataloguing exits, timing the distance between seated passengers, and lingering on any man whose posture feels too still. She watches them closely, reading every shift in weight, every glance toward the door. She is certain that threat is always one missed cue away. Her conviction that the world is fundamentally unsafe sits beside her certainty that she cannot manage even the slightest upset without collapsing. These beliefs do not explain one another; they simply occupy her mind alongside the sudden, unbidden reliving of the event. The patterns shape her work. When an old client emails a photograph of a renovated space they visited years ago, Linh stares at the background until she can no longer breathe, her chest tightening as the image pulls her back to the crowd outside the restaurant. More often, the scent of alcohol derails her days. During a walkthrough for a new hotel lobby, a contractor stepped onto the loading dock and returned with the familiar, heavy odor of beer clinging to his jacket. Linh abruptly dropped her measuring tape, walked to the stairwell, and sat on the concrete steps until her hands stopped trembling. She has stopped accepting client dinners, telling herself she simply lacks the energy for socializing, though the truth is she fears the clink of glass and the murmur of crowded rooms. Alongside these sensations, other rhythms have taken root. When her thoughts fracture into the smell of smoke and the sound of screaming, she pins her fingers with a straight pin until the sharp, clean sting overpowers the chaos. In the mornings, she runs ten miles before dawn, pushing her legs past exhaustion until her body feels too heavy to carry the day. When the urge to escape her own mind becomes too strong, she sits at her kitchen island and eats plain rice and toast until her stomach aches, using the weight of the food to ground herself. These habits formed quietly, week by week, becoming the only architecture she trusts to hold her together. It was the morning she realized she could not finish a presentation for a major municipal contract-her hands shaking so badly she could not unclip her portfolio, her mind fixed on the contractor's jacket from last week-that Linh finally called a therapist's office. She told the receptionist she wanted to stop running before she runs out of places to hide. What she hopes for is quiet; what she fears most is that the world will keep turning toward danger, and she will keep breaking beneath it.
